scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Flower of the Joseon Court
This is Chunaengjeon. 17th-19th century.
on_screen: Hero video — MISSING
Title card: Chunaengjeon · South Korea · 17th-19th century

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The oldest text mentioning Chunaengjeon is the Jinchan Uigwe (Manual of Court Banquet) of 1848, which notes that the dance existed in the Joseon court from 1649.
It was revised and perfected under Crown Prince Hyomyeong and performed for Queen Sunwon's 40th birthday in 1828.
Jinchan Uigwe cites the 1701 Chinese encyclopedia Yuanchien Leihan, noting Emperor Gaozong of Tang ordered musician Po Ming Chien to compose music inspired by a nightingale.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally created and performed for royal court banquets (jeongjae), such as Queen Sunwon's birthday in 1828, the dance signifies the arrival of spring and poetically represents the movements of an oriole.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Chunaengjeon is performed as a solo dance entirely on a woven floral mat called a hwamunseok.
The dancer moves back and forth and turns around using defined and controlled steps without stepping off the mat.
Dancers wear traditional beoseon socks instead of shoes.
Watch for hwajeontae.
on_screen: Hero video — MISSING
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Solo performance strictly confined to a single floral-patterned straw mat (hwamunseok).
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance is accompanied by the classical Korean court music composition pyeongjo hoesang.
Historical lyrics associated with its Chinese predecessor express poetic themes: 'Walking in the moonlight, wind through sleeves, standing before a flower, yearning for a lover'.
Listen for the Korean court instruments.
Accompanied by the traditional Korean court music suite pyeongjo hoesang, presenting a slow, refined classical atmosphere suited to Joseon royal banquets.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: The soloist wears a yellow gown called an aengsam and performs without shoes, wearing only white beoseon socks.
Male dancers wear a lotus coronet headdress, while female dancers wear a jokduri headdress.
The physical performance space is restricted to a decorative straw mat with floral patterns (hwamunseok).

scenes.title: The people
narration: Crown Prince Hyomyeong revised and perfected the dance in the late Joseon period.
Emperor Sunjong observed performances in the early 20th century.
Derived from Joseon royal court dance (jeongjae) traditions, referencing older Tang Dynasty nightingale dance precedents recorded in Chinese encyclopedias.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Chunaengjeon is sibling of Cheoyongmu: One of the five Korean court dances preserved during the Japanese occupation.
Chunaengjeon is sibling of Mugo: One of five court dances preserved through the occupation alongside Chunaengjeon.
Chunaengjeon is sibling of Pogurak: Shared survival as a traditional court dance (jeongjae) into the modern era.
Chunaengjeon is sibling of Geommu: Korean court dance preserved alongside Chunaengjeon.
